prose: Undercharging split coke caused the operational coke bed to burn down 30cm below optimal tuyere height. The melting zone dropped into the lower oxidizing zone; the tapped gray iron chilled to 1,340°C, mis-running thin machine tool gearbox castings.

Charging 45 kg of high-calcium limestone per ton of scrap iron yielded a brilliant, honey-colored, free-flowing fluid slag. The basic CaO-SiO2 slag flushed cleanly through the rear slag notch, scrubbing ash and preventing tuyere fouling.

Oversized sheared rail sections wedged tightly against refractory wall linings, forming a rigid hanging bridge halfway up the stack. Below the scaffold, bed coke burned out completely; blast had to be killed while melters poked the bridge down with steel bars.

A blower belt slip dropped windbox pressure from 8 kPa to 3 kPa. Slag splashing across the tuyere noses froze into glassy black stalactites, blocking four out of six blast ports and severely distorting combustion air symmetry.

Droplets of melted steel scrap trickling down through eighteen inches of incandescent coke picked up 2.8% carbon before collecting in the well. The high-carbon iron tapped at 1,450°C with exceptional fluidity, perfectly filling complex radiator patterns.

Adding 0.3% crushed 75% ferrosilicon into the tapping stream nucleated dense Type-A flake graphite. Chill wedge test samples showed zero hard white iron along the sharp edge, ensuring all pump housings could be turned and drilled without dulling tool bits.

Knocking out the prop under the bottom hinged iron doors dumped five tons of incandescent coke bed and molten slag onto the dry sand pit floor below. Rapid water spraying quenched the glowing drop, clearing the shaft for morning refractory re-patching.

Scavenged high-sulfur foundry coke (1.3% S) elevated iron sulfur content to a hazardous 0.16%. Injecting granular calcium carbide via a porous nitrogen plug in the holding ladle dropped sulfur to 0.025%, preventing brittle iron hot shortness.
